body.text: Attribution: M.U. Nair, “The AI Handler Doctrine: A Framework for Operational AI Accountability,” ORF Special Report No. 322, Observer Research Foundation, September 2026.

Every consequential institutional domain in modern societies has a designated supervisory authority at the point of decision. Medical professionals are accountable for clinical judgements, auditors sign off on financial statements, military commanders bear responsibility for operational orders, and judges are bound by law and subject to appellate review.

Artificial intelligence (AI) does not yet operate within a comparable structure. Even as AI systems now influence governance decisions, clinical diagnoses, credit assessments, intelligence analyses, and law-enforcement outcomes, no clearly designated authority exists to verify whether those outputs are contextually appropriate, current, representative, or sufficiently reliable for the use to which they are being put. This is not primarily a technical problem. The AI research community has produced substantial work on transparency, explainability, fairness, and safety. International bodies such as the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development[1] (OECD), United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization[2] (UNESCO), and the European Union[3] (EU) have developed governance principles.

These contributions are valuable; however, they address what AI systems should achieve, not who bears operational accountability when outputs are deployed in critical environments and something goes wrong. When harmful or misleading AI output emerges from a complex deployment chain involving a model developer, a cloud provider, a system integrator, a data provider, and an end-user institution, existing frameworks leave accountability fragmented across all, and more importantly, enforceable against none of them, at the moment it matters. This report proposes the AI Handler Doctrine to address that gap.

Not all AI systems require identical accountability obligations, and the AI Handler framework should not be understood as being universally applicable. The question is, what distinguishes an AI system that warrants formal supervisory accountability from one that does not? Three criteria, applied cumulatively, define the threshold.

This refers to the potential for an AI output, if erroneous, biased, or contextually misaligned, to produce gross harm to individuals, institutions, or public systems. A credit assessment that determines loan eligibility for millions of citizens carries a consequence of magnitude. However, a recommendation engine suggesting weekend reading does not.

This applies to the scale at which the system operates. AI systems embedded within public digital infrastructure, population-scale services, or national governance platforms affect large numbers of people simultaneously. An error propagated at that scale is categorically different from an error in a contained institutional system.

This applies to the degree to which AI-influenced decisions are difficult to contest, reverse, or appeal once made. Automated decisions in law enforcement, judicial support, welfare eligibility, or healthcare diagnostics carry higher irreversibility than decisions in contexts where human review is routine and accessible.

A system that meets all three criteria—one that acknowledges the critical consequence magnitude, broad population reach, and limited decision reversibility—falls within the scope of the AI Handler framework. A system that meets only one criterion may warrant lighter transparency obligations but not the full supervisory architecture. Meanwhile, a system that meets none requires only basic disclosure.

This framework of societal and sovereign-scale AI systems should be applied across all platforms whose outputs materially influence public administration, healthcare and public health systems, financial services and economic decision-making, critical infrastructure, national security and defence, law enforcement, judicial processes, and population-scale digital public infrastructure.

Personal productivity tools, entertainment and content recommendation systems, internal decision support tools whose outputs are always subject to direct human review, and limited automation systems with no consequential external outputs are explicitly outside the scope of the full Handler obligation.

The framework also recognises that the same underlying AI model may operate across multiple categories, depending on deployment context. A large language model (LLM) used to draft internal correspondence may not necessitate AI Handler obligations. The same model integrated into a judicial support system, a welfare service eligibility platform, or a defence intelligence system, does. The trigger is, therefore, the deployment context and function, not the model itself.
This follows a principle of proportionate accountability where oversight obligations scale with the severity of consequences, not with the level of technological sophistication.

Over the past decade, governments, international organisations, and technology companies have produced substantial AI governance frameworks. The New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact, adopted at the India AI Impact Summit and endorsed by 89 countries and major international organisations, promotes the democratic diffusion, equitable access, and responsible development of AI. While these contributions are important, they do not address the absence of a designated supervisory authority accountable and responsible for validating AI outputs at the moment of consequential use.
There are four structural reasons:

The frameworks and principles promulgated by nations establish what AI systems should aspire to be, which are fairness, transparency, and accountability in the abstract sense. They do not designate who, within a specific operational environment, is responsible for verifying whether a particular output meets those standards before it influences a consequential decision.

Commercial contracts between AI developers, deployers, and users can and do allocate liability. However, contractual accountability is structurally reactive since it provides recourse only after harm has occurred, through dispute resolution, compensation, or termination. It does not create a supervisory presence within the operational decision chain. By the time contractual remedies are invoked, the harmful output has already influenced a decision. In critical domains, an incorrect diagnosis, a wrongful credit denial affecting livelihood, or an intelligence assessment that shapes an operational order may have severe consequences.

Professional liability frameworks hold practitioners, including doctors, lawyers, and financial advisors, accountable for their judgements. However, these frameworks were designed for environments where a professional exercises independent judgement and one can assess the basis for their decisions. AI systems increasingly compress or obscure that process. When a clinician relies on an AI-generated diagnostic recommendation, or a loan officer acts on an algorithmically produced credit score, the professional's liability does not automatically extend to the AI output itself. The originating system, its training data, its contextual assumptions, and its confidence calibration remain outside the scope of professional accountability as currently structured.

Competition and reputational pressure can, over time, reward responsible AI deployment and penalise harmful products. However, market feedback mechanisms operate at timescales and granularities incompatible with the oversight requirements of high-consequence AI deployments. A pattern of AI-driven errors in welfare entitlement decisions may take years to become visible in aggregate data. By the time market correction occurs, millions of individual decisions will have already been made. Markets also respond to visible, attributable failures since they are poorly equipped to address harms that are systemic, diffuse, or difficult to attribute to a specific AI output.

The challenge is not a lack of principles but the absence of an operational accountability architecture. What is missing is a designated supervisory mechanism that sits within the deployment chain itself. An accountable entity operates in real time to check whether a specific AI output is contextually appropriate, sufficiently reliable, and fit for the consequential use to which it is being put. This is what the AI Handler framework is designed to provide.

Before any supervisory architecture can function effectively, a prior and more fundamental obligation must be met: AI platforms themselves must be held accountable for what their systems produce. This is currently not the case. AI platforms operating at societal scale today deliver outputs, clinical recommendations, legal interpretations, financial assessments, and governance analyses, all without disclosing the informational basis, geographic provenance, demographic coverage, or confidence reliability of those outputs to the institutions and individuals relying on them. Users receive responses presented with uniform confidence, regardless of whether the underlying data sets are comprehensive or narrow, current or outdated, globally representative or geographically concentrated. This is not solely a technical limitation; it is also a disclosure and accountability challenge.

At an internal level, platforms already possess the information necessary to characterise their outputs honestly. They know which data sets their systems were trained on, and their geographic and demographic composition. They are aware of the confidence distribution of their retrieval systems, as well as where their training data is sparse, where it is concentrated, and where it reflects institutional assumptions drawn from certain national or cultural contexts. The barrier to surfacing this information is not technical incapability; it is the absence of any enforceable obligation to do so.
The accountability burden must be borne by the system that produced the output, not by an institutional layer built around the system's silence about its own limitations.

This report proposes that AI platforms operating at societal or sovereign scale be required to meet three categories of output-level disclosure as a condition of deployment in high-consequence environments.

For any output in a high-consequence domain, the platform must disclose the primary sources, geographic coverage, and demographic composition of the data sets informing that output. This does not require platforms to publish proprietary training data. It requires them to characterise, at the output level, what their systems know and from where they got the information. A response that draws predominantly on United States (US) regulatory data bases should say so. A clinical recommendation based on patient details from Western Europe should say so. A legal interpretation derived from common law jurisdictions should say so when delivered in a civil law context.

Platforms must disclose the confidence distribution of their outputs, distinguishing between well-documented responses, responses based on limited or dated data, and responses that involve inference or extrapolation beyond the training data set. This is not an invitation to arbitrarily undermine user confidence; it is a requirement that confidence be calibrated accurately rather than presented uniformly. An output generated from sparse or unrepresentative data should not be delivered with the same apparent authority as an output generated from comprehensive, current, and contextually relevant sources.

Where a platform's training data reflects legal, institutional, cultural, or governance assumptions that differ materially from the deployment context, this must be flagged at the output level. A platform trained predominantly on US healthcare protocols delivering recommendations to a doctor in Kerala or trained on European financial regulation delivering compliance guidance to a fintech operating under the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) norms, must disclose that its contextual assumptions may not transfer reliably. The user, whether a medical professional, a lawyer, an administrator, or a policymaker, must be informed of the gap between the system's trained context and the deployment context.

These are market access conditions, not aspirations. These three obligations are not requests for voluntary disclosures. They are proposed as mandatory conditions for AI platforms seeking to operate at societal or sovereign scale within a nation’s information ecosystem.

Platforms that cannot demonstrate compliance with baseline output accountability standards and cannot characterise the provenance of their outputs, calibrate their confidence disclosures, or flag material contextual limitations, should not be permitted to operate in high-consequence institutional environments. This is not technological protectionism.

In a country like India, market scale gives AI genuine leverage. Platforms that wish to operate within the nation's healthcare system, financial infrastructure, public administration, and digital public infrastructure must meet the standards it sets. The European Union (EU) has demonstrated that jurisdictional scale translates into regulatory norm setting at the global level. India's digital scale, the world's largest population of internet users, and the world's most sophisticated digital public infrastructure (DPI) undoubtedly provide equivalent leverage when deliberately exercised.

Mandatory epistemic transparency places the accountability burden for output reliability squarely where it belongs: on the platform that produces the output. This is a more assertive and fundamental demand than the Handler framework alone.

This does not, however, eliminate the need for deployment context supervision. A platform can disclose that its clinical data sets draw predominantly from European patient cohorts. It cannot determine whether—given that limitation and given the specific patient, setting, and clinical circumstances at hand—the output should be acted upon, qualified, or escalated. That judgement requires someone with knowledge of the deployment environment, like the local disease burden, the available resources, the institutional protocols, and the patient's specific circumstances.

This is what the AI Handler provides: not compensation for a platform's failure to disclose its limitations, but the deployment context judgement that no platform, however transparent, can substitute for. Platform accountability and Handler supervision are, therefore, sequential obligations, not alternatives. The first ensures that platforms are honest about what they know and do not know. The second ensures that institutions deploying AI outputs are accountable for whether those outputs are appropriate for the specific consequential decisions they inform. Together, they constitute a complete operational accountability framework. Neither is sufficient by itself.

A common objection to operational AI accountability frameworks is that supervisory requirements will slow deployment, increase compliance costs, and disadvantage innovation, particularly for smaller platforms and emerging economies. This concern deserves a direct response.
The AI Handler framework is designed to be innovation-compatible through three structural choices.

First, it operates at the deployment, not at the development level: The framework does not regulate how AI systems are built, what architectures they use, how they are trained, or what capabilities they develop. It applies at the point of consequential use, when an AI output is being acted upon in a high-stakes institutional environment. A research laboratory, a product team, or a startup developing AI capabilities faces no Handler obligation until and unless the system is deployed in a societal or sovereign-scale environment. Development, experimentation, and iteration remain entirely unaffected.

Second, it is proportionate by design: Handler obligations scale with the severity of consequence. Personal productivity tools, entertainment systems, and internal automation with direct human review and limited-function applications carry only basic transparency obligations. Full supervisory architecture applies only to systems meeting the threshold criteria defined earlier. Most AI deployments, by volume, if not by consequence, may fall outside the full framework.

Third, accountability historically enables innovation at scale, rather than suppressing it. Aviation did not become a smaller industry because of certification requirements. It became the infrastructure of global commerce because certification created the institutional trust that made mass adoption possible. Financial markets did not contract under prudential regulation; supervisory frameworks allowed the expansion of credit, capital markets, and financial services to populations that could not previously access them. In each case, accountability structures solved the trust problem that constrained adoption, and adoption then accelerated.

AI faces an analogous trust problem. The principal barrier to deeper AI integration in healthcare, public administration, defence, and critical infrastructure is not technical capability. It is institutional confidence that AI outputs are reliable, contextually appropriate, and supervised by someone accountable when they are not. A framework that credibly answers that question does not constrain AI adoption. It is the condition under which consequential AI adoption can occur responsibly.

The concern is not entirely without merit in one respect. Compliance costs are real and poorly designed accountability frameworks can impose disproportionate burdens on smaller platforms. This is addressed directly in the implementation section through phased obligations and size-proportionate requirements. The objective is not a uniform burden but calibrated responsibility, the same principle that governs financial regulation, pharmaceutical approvals, and aviation certification across entities of very different scale.
The most important challenge facing contemporary AI systems is not necessarily what they get wrong; it is often what they systematically fail to recognise.

Representation Gaps: Large AI systems are predominantly trained using data ecosystems shaped by digitally visible, commercially indexed, and technologically mature environments. This creates risks that perspectives from developing economies, indigenous knowledge systems, local governance models, and non-Western institutional experiences may receive comparatively lower visibility. This may not necessarily be the result of deliberate exclusion. Rather, it reflects the structural characteristics of global data production and digital representation.
However, as AI increasingly influences public discourse and decision-making, unequal visibility can shape perceptions of legitimacy and authority, often changing outcomes.

Attribution Challenges: AI systems increasingly synthesise vast volumes of information while often providing limited visibility into intellectual origins. Attribution concerns extend beyond academic recognition; they affect source traceability, policy accountability, intellectual property considerations, and the representation of diverse knowledge traditions.
As machine-mediated knowledge becomes increasingly influential, attribution integrity becomes a component of digital trust.

Contextual Misalignment: Many AI systems are trained on data sets reflecting legal, cultural, economic, and institutional assumptions developed in particular national environments or geographies. As a result, responses to questions originating from countries such as India may sometimes reflect regulatory assumptions, social contexts, or institutional frameworks that differ markedly from local realities. In areas such as healthcare, law, public administration, or governance, contextual misalignment may produce recommendations that are technically coherent but operationally inappropriate.

Operational Risks: Generative AI systems can also exhibit hallucinations, information staleness, overconfidence, incomplete contextual awareness, or at times, retrieval limitations. These challenges become increasingly important when AI outputs influence important decisions. This does not mean questioning whether AI systems should be used; it must be ensured that they are deployed within accountable supervisory frameworks capable of identifying and mitigating such limitations.

The AI Handler Doctrine proposes that AI systems operating within high-consequence environments should incorporate structured operational accountability mechanisms. The AI Handler is at the centre of this framework.

The AI Handler is a designated supervisory authority responsible for: reviewing AI outputs; assessing contextual appropriateness; evaluating uncertainty indicators; verifying attribution integrity; monitoring representational fairness; escalating high-risk decisions; and conducting accountability reviews

It is not intended to function merely as a compliance officer or auditor. Auditors typically assess systems periodically. Regulators establish external governance requirements. The AI Handler functions within the operational decision chain itself, providing continuous supervisory accountability during deployment.

The AI Handler is a functional role rather than a fixed institutional entity. Depending on the deployment context, the Handler may be platform-embedded or institution-embedded, situated within the organisation deploying AI at the customer premises itself, such as a hospital, financial institution, government agency, or defence organisation. It could also be an independent third party, provided through an accredited organisation, or a specialised audit entity. However, it needs to be recognised by sector-specific regulatory frameworks in sensitive environments. The appropriate model should be determined according to sectoral sensitivity and consequence severity.
The AI Handler performs several core functions. It could range from:
• Output validation by reviewing high-risk AI outputs before consequential implementation
• Context assessment ensuring that recommendations align with local legal, cultural, institutional, and operational realities
• Carrying out attribution review by assessing source traceability and representational integrity
• Ensuring uncertainty assessment by evaluating confidence levels, assumptions, and limitations
• Catering for escalation management by referring high-consequence decisions for additional review
• Supporting grievance redressal by monitoring supporting-user reviews, appeals, and accountability processes
• Assisting in audit processes by maintaining accountability records and ensuring accountability reporting by providing periodic assessments of system performance and emerging risks

The AI Handler framework does not require a single individual to hold simultaneous expertise across all domains of deployment. That expectation would be neither realistic nor necessary. What the framework requires, instead, is a tiered team structure in which accountability is distributed across three levels, each with a defined role.

At the first tier, every Handler structure requires a standing AI governance competence—professionals with working knowledge of how AI systems behave operationally, including their failure modes, confidence calibration characteristics, hallucination patterns, attribution limitations, and contextual constraints. This is the Handler's core standing function, regardless of deployment sector, and the foundation upon which sector-specific supervision is built.

At the second tier, domain specialists need to be engaged for sector-specific oversight—clinical professionals for healthcare deployments, financial risk professionals for credit and market systems, legal specialists for judicial support environments, and operational specialists for defence and security contexts. These specialists need not be permanently embedded within every Handler team. For many deployments, they will function as designated advisors engaged for specific high-consequence outputs, much as an institution's legal function retains specialist external counsel for domain-specific matters while maintaining standing in-house counsel for routine governance.

At the third tier, for the highest-consequence deployments—those meeting all three threshold criteria of consequence magnitude, population reach, and decision irreversibility—governance boards should provide periodic oversight and audit, drawing on interdisciplinary expertise across law, ethics, technology, and sector-specific regulation.

This distribution of expertise resolves a practical tension that the framework would otherwise face: no single person can simultaneously be an AI engineer, a clinician, a financial regulator, and a defence analyst. The Handler chain as a whole holds the required expertise. The framework applies the same logic: the burden of accountability is not delegated to the machine; it is held by a structured human chain, at every level of which someone is responsible for what the AI outputs are allowed to influence.

Pillar I: Integrity Assurance

AI systems frequently generate outputs based on outdated, incomplete, or geographically distorted information while presenting them with unwarranted confidence. In key domains and critical infrastructures, informational staleness can create strategic harm. Under the mandatory disclosure obligations established in this framework, AI systems operating in highly sensitive environments are required to provide: Knowledge vintage disclosure; Confidence transparency; Dataset geography indicators; Uncertainty signalling; and Contextual limitation alerts.

Accountability architectures must evolve towards continuous and adaptive auditability, capable of assessing behavioural drift, retrieval evolution, model updates, and emergent operational risks over specified periods. An AI system incapable of indicating the reliability, representativeness, or freshness of its informational base must not be treated as an authoritative operational instrument in critical environments. Platforms operating in such environments are required to incorporate AI Handler-supportive interface mechanisms that can expose confidence levels, uncertainty indicators, contextual limitations, and operational alerts necessary for supervisory human evaluation. These are not optional enhancements; they are baseline operating requirements.[4]
Pillar II: Attribution Integrity

AI systems increasingly absorb, synthesise, and reproduce intellectual constructs without correctly identifying their originators. This disproportionately disadvantages Global South research efforts, indigenous strategic thought, non-Western policy innovation, and locally evolved governance frameworks. The AI Handler architecture, therefore, proposes attribution traceability mechanisms, indigenous concepts registries, institutional safeguards against silent intellectual erasure, and context-sensitive source transparency. In the age of machine-generated and machine-mediated cognition, attribution becomes inseparable from epistemic sovereignty.
Pillar III: Contextual Sovereignty

AI systems trained predominantly on Western data sets frequently interpret global realities through Western institutional, legal, cultural, and geopolitical assumptions. Queries originating from India, Africa, Southeast Asia, or Latin America often receive responses framed through US regulatory logic, European governance assumptions, or Western strategic paradigms, even where local frameworks fundamentally differ. Many local repositories and publicly available knowledge resources may receive limited visibility within prevailing retrieval architectures prior to result generation. This may create governance misalignment and strategic dependency, and in sectors such as healthcare, potentially inappropriate diagnostic or treatment pathways. The delivery of services to citizens may be distorted by inappropriate responses provided by the AI platform.

Contextual sovereignty, therefore, refers to the ability of AI systems to reflect local legal, cultural, linguistic, institutional, and governance realities. For countries such as India, contextual relevance requires: Multilingual capabilities; Local knowledge integration; Regional representation; and Institutionally relevant retrieval mechanisms.

AI systems should not merely provide technically accurate answers; they should provide answers appropriate to the environment in which they are deployed. This challenge reflects a deployment context mismatch in which systems optimised for one institutional environment may become less reliable when applied across substantially different socio-economic, legal, linguistic, and governance settings. Contextual sovereignty concerns the relevance of AI outputs, whereas cognitive sovereignty concerns a society's capacity to interpret and act upon knowledge through its own institutional frameworks
The AI Handler architecture mandates sovereign contextualisation, multilingual calibration, geographically aware retrieval structures, and local institutional integration.
Pillar IV: Accountability Architecture

AI systems today operate with diffused responsibility. When harmful, misleading, biased, or operationally damaging outputs emerge, accountability frequently becomes fragmented across model developers, deployment platforms, retrieval systems, integrators, and end users.

The AI Handler Doctrine proposes a formal operational chain of responsibility comprising platform operators, supervisory AI Handler teams, domain specialists, and governance boards with audit authorities and grievance redressal mechanisms.

Every leading AI platform should designate a registered AI Handler authority who will be responsible for operational oversight, post-output audit, contextual validation, bias review, escalation protocols, user grievance handling, and periodic accountability reporting. In practice, AI Handler functions are unlikely to be exercised by a single individual. Significant and sensitive environments may require multidisciplinary teams comprising domain specialists, AI practitioners, legal experts, risk managers, and governance professionals capable of collectively evaluating operational implications.
Pillar V: Responsible and Unbiased Behaviour

AI neutrality is often assumed but rarely examined, and therefore, all AI systems inherit structural bias from data composition, language dominance, retrieval hierarchies, institutional assumptions, and even training methodologies. The issue is not whether bias exists, but whether it is measured, disclosed, and operationally mitigated. As a user, one needs to be made aware of how the response was generated or how a solution came to evolve.

Responsible AI behaviour must, therefore, extend beyond aspirational ethical declarations. AI systems would need to distinguish fact from inference, disclose uncertainty, avoid manipulative amplification, minimise ideological and geopolitical skew, respect sovereign legal and cultural contexts, and maintain measurable diversity in source representation. In addition, individuals and institutions materially affected by consequential AI-generated assessments should possess access to meaningful review, contestability, and grievance redressal mechanisms capable of enabling accountable human reassessment.

While integrity assurance focuses on the quality and reliability of AI outputs, accountability architecture focuses on the allocation of responsibility when those outputs influence consequential decisions. It needs to be ensured that no AI system operating at sovereign or global scale should remain beyond meaningful scrutiny.

The AI Handler framework, therefore, proposes measurable behavioural accountability standards capable of evaluating representational fairness, contextual legitimacy, and attributional integrity, besides operational reliability. Concerns regarding linguistic underrepresentation, data-set concentration, and uneven visibility of Global South knowledge ecosystems have increasingly been highlighted within international discussions on AI governance, digital inclusion, and responsible AI development, including by UNESCO, the OECD, and various multilateral digital governance forums.

The concept of an AI Handler necessitates sovereign nations to progressively integrate operational AI accountability into their digital governance frameworks. This ensures the legitimacy to enable universal roll-out across information domains. It should not be framed as technological protectionism or censorship. Rather, it should be understood as a sovereign digital safety requirement that is analogous to certifications or sector regulatory compliance mandates. In fact, governments today are already imposing operational standards on technologies that affect public safety, national security, economic stability, and societal trust. And AI systems increasingly meet all four criteria.

Sovereign jurisdictions may, therefore, progressively require AI platforms operating within their information ecosystems to comply with legally enforceable accountability obligations, which include registered AI Handler structures, contextual accountability mechanisms, attribution traceability and bias audit frameworks, human-in-the-loop supervisory architectures, and grievance redressal systems.

Platforms operating in critical environments may also be increasingly required to maintain operational transparency instruments capable of supporting AI Handler supervision mechanisms, including contextual disclosure frameworks, audit support frameworks, and supervisory interface structures. Depending on the deployment context, AI Handlers may be designated by platform operators, recognised by sectoral regulators, or certified through sovereign accountability frameworks.

In the future, market access for AI platforms may increasingly become conditional upon adherence to operational standards for accountability. This would represent a normal evolutionary process of sovereign digital governance and not a technological exclusion.

The AI Handler framework is designed for phased implementation, allowing institutions, platforms, and regulatory bodies time to build the necessary structures and capabilities. The phasing follows a logic of progressive obligation: each phase builds on the preceding one and no phase imposes requirements that the previous phase has not built towards. The compliance burden is explicitly calibrated across phases—earlier phases impose lighter obligations, allowing smaller platforms and less resource-intensive institutions to establish baseline capability before higher-consequence obligations take effect.
Phase I: Transparency Disclosure

In the first phase, governments should require AI platforms operating in India to meet baseline disclosure standards, specifically the disclosure of data currency and knowledge vintage, geographic and demographic coverage of training data sets, jurisdictional assumptions embedded in outputs, bias mitigation approaches in place, and the identity and contact of the designated accountability representative. These disclosures should be made publicly available in standardised formats. Phase I obligations should apply to all platforms operating at sovereign scale, regardless of size. The disclosure standard is light enough that even smaller platforms can meet it without disproportionate compliance costs. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) should develop the disclosure standard and registry framework within 12 months of policy adoption.
Phase II: Accountability Registration

In the second phase, large-scale AI platforms—those exceeding the defined thresholds of user reach, deployment consequence, or sectoral penetration—would be required to designate registered AI Handler authorities, establish local compliance representation within India, publish annual accountability audit reports, and implement grievance redressal frameworks accessible to affected users. Smaller platforms meeting lower thresholds will be required to demonstrate Phase I compliance and designate a named accountability contact but are not yet subject to the full Handler registration requirement. This size-proportionate distinction is deliberate: the framework imposes heavier obligations where consequential reach is greatest, and lighter obligations where it is not. Sector regulators—the RBI, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI), the National Medical Commission (NMC), the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)—should register Handler authorities within their domains, while MeitY maintains the national registry.
Phase III: High-Risk Sector Regulation

In the third phase, AI systems operating in defined high-consequence environments—healthcare diagnostics, financial credit and insurance, law enforcement analytics, welfare eligibility, judicial support, and critical infrastructure—would be required to certify operational accountability compliance. This certification covers Handler team establishment, tiered expertise structure, mandatory disclosure compliance, human-in-the-loop protocols for irreversible decisions, and grievance redressal accessibility. Non-certified platforms will not be permitted to operate in these environments. Sector regulators can develop and administer certification frameworks within their domains. The IndiaAI Mission can provide technical standards support.[5]
Phase IV: Sovereign Certification

In the fourth and final phase, AI systems seeking to operate at large scale, integrated with DPI platforms, national security systems, or population-scale public services, would be required to comply with nationally mandated operational accountability standards and undergo sovereign certification. Sovereign certification adds requirements beyond sector-level compliance: demonstrated training data adequacy for the Indian population, contextual validation against Indian institutional frameworks, multilingual capability for relevant deployment contexts, and attribution integrity mechanisms. Platforms that achieve sovereign certification will be recognised as meeting India's highest standard for responsible AI deployment. This certification carries implications for international recognition. India should work through multilateral forums to promote interoperability, mutual recognition, and cross-jurisdictional acceptance of sovereign AI accountability standards, thereby reducing regulatory fragmentation while preserving national governance priorities

The phased structure ensures that the compliance burden is proportionate at every stage. No platform faces the full accountability architecture from day one. Every platform faces obligations commensurate with the consequences of its deployments, which is precisely the principle of proportionate accountability that governs the entire framework.

India occupies a distinctive position in the global AI ecosystem. Unlike many countries that are primarily consumers of AI technologies, India simultaneously possesses the scale, digital infrastructure, institutional depth, and policy experience necessary to shape emerging AI governance norms.[6]

India's digital public infrastructure (DPI) ecosystem—including Aadhaar, unified payments interface (UPI), Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC), and other population-scale platforms—already serves hundreds of millions of citizens. As AI systems become integrated into these platforms, questions of accountability, contextual relevance, and transparency acquire national significance. A contextual failure embedded within such systems is not merely a technological malfunction; it becomes a governance challenge affecting large populations.

India is also uniquely positioned to contribute to global AI governance discussions from the perspective of the Global South. Many developing societies face concerns regarding contextual relevance, linguistic diversity, representational equity, and institutional compatibility that are not always adequately addressed by governance models developed elsewhere. The AI Handler framework seeks to address these concerns through accountability, attribution integrity, contextual sovereignty, and operational supervision.

At the same time, India has an opportunity to advance sovereign AI capabilities through initiatives such as the IndiaAI Mission and BharatGen. The long-term objective should not merely be the deployment of foreign AI systems within India, but the development of AI ecosystems trained, validated, and governed using Indian data sets, languages, institutional frameworks, and accountability standards.

The broader objective is cognitive sovereignty: the ability of a nation to interpret, govern, and make decisions through frameworks grounded in its own institutional, cultural, and strategic realities. As AI increasingly mediates knowledge, decision-making, and public discourse, preserving this capacity will become an important component of national resilience and digital self-determination. Cognitive sovereignty should be distinguished from data sovereignty. While data sovereignty concerns the ownership, storage, processing, and legal control of data, cognitive sovereignty concerns the frameworks through which that data is interpreted and transformed into knowledge, recommendations, and decisions. A nation may possess complete control over its data while remaining dependent on external institutional assumptions, analytical models, and decision-support architectures. Cognitive sovereignty, therefore, addresses the ability of societies to understand and act upon their realities through frameworks that reflect their own legal, cultural, institutional, and strategic contexts. India's choices over the coming decade will, therefore, influence not only its own AI future but potentially the governance trajectory of AI across many developing societies facing similar challenges.

India also possesses institutional depth uniquely suited to operational AI accountability architectures, including experienced civil services, strategic communities, public health institutions, judicial systems, and defence establishments, all of which are capable of providing the domain expertise necessary for responsible AI supervision.
The AI Handler Doctrine offers one possible pathway towards restoring that balance.[7]

The following recommendations are organised across the three layers of the AI accountability framework proposed in this paper. They are intended as a sequenced roadmap, not an undifferentiated list. Tier 1 establishes the foundational platform obligations that make subsequent layers meaningful; Tier 2 builds the operational supervisory architecture; and Tier 3 addresses India's long-term sovereign AI development agenda.
These recommendations establish mandatory disclosure and accountability standards as market access conditions for AI platforms operating at scale in India.[8]
Responsible Actor: MeitY, in coordination with sector regulators.

AI platforms operating in high-consequence domains—healthcare, financial services, public administration, law enforcement, defence, and critical infrastructure—must be required to disclose, at the output level, the primary sources, geographic coverage, and demographic composition of the data sets informing that output. This is not a requirement to publish proprietary training data; it is to characterise, honestly and specifically, what the system knows and from where. MeitY should develop the disclosure standard, and sector regulators should enforce it within their domains.

Platforms must be required to distinguish, at the output level, between well-evidenced responses, responses based on limited or dated data, and responses that involve inference beyond the training data set. Uniform confidence presentation—the current default—should be prohibited in high-consequence deployment environments. The Bureau of Indian Standards, in consultation with MeitY and the IndiaAI Mission, should develop the technical standard for confidence calibration.

Wherever a platform's training data reflects legal, institutional, or cultural assumptions that differ materially from the Indian deployment context, it must be disclosed at the output level. Policymakers may consider restricting the deployment of platforms that cannot demonstrate compliance with baseline output accountability standards in high-consequence institutional environments. The objective is not to limit innovation but to ensure that consequential deployments meet the minimum standards of transparency and accountability. Sector regulators—IRDAI, RBI, NMC, MHA—should each develop sector-specific contextual adequacy standards for AI systems operating within their domains.

All AI platforms operating at societal or sovereign scale in India should be required to register with a designated authority, publish annual accountability reports covering output accuracy assessments, bias audit findings, contextual limitation disclosures, and grievance redressal performance. MeitY should establish the registration framework and the IndiaAI Mission should maintain the registry.[9]
These recommendations establish the operational supervisory infrastructure for AI deployment in high-consequence environments.
Responsible Actors: Sector ministries and regulators, with a national coordination function under MeitY.
• Establish AI Handler Structures in High-Risk Sectors

The Ministries of Health, Finance, Home Affairs, Defence, and Law, in coordination with their respective sector regulators, should each mandate the establishment of AI Handler teams within institutions deploying AI in high-consequence operational environments. Handler teams should follow the tiered model described in this paper: a standing AI governance competence, sector-specific domain specialists, and governance board oversight for the highest-consequence deployments. The IndiaAI Mission should develop the Handler certification framework.

AI systems influencing decisions that are difficult to contest, reverse, or appeal—welfare eligibility determinations, clinical diagnoses acting as primary inputs to treatment, credit assessments for populations with limited financial history, law enforcement risk assessments—must be required to incorporate designated human supervisory review before those decisions are implemented. This is not a requirement for the human review of every AI output. It highlights the need for human sign-off on the specific category of outputs where AI error causes disproportionate and difficult-to-remedy harm. Sector regulators should define the specific decision categories within their domains.[10]

Individuals and institutions materially affected by consequential AI-generated assessments should have access to meaningful, accessible, and time-bound review and contestability processes. These mechanisms should be sector-specific—a health grievance pathway differs from a financial services pathway—but should meet common minimum standards for accessibility, transparency, and response time. The Consumer Affairs Ministry, in coordination with sector regulators, should develop the framework.

The IndiaAI Mission, in consultation with the NMC, RBI, relevant defence establishments, and other sector bodies, should develop the certification standards for AI Handler team competencies—both the AI governance literacy required of all Handler team members and the domain expertise standards required for sector-specific supervisory roles. India's Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs), Indian Institutes of Management (IIMs), and National Law Universities (NLUs) are well-placed to develop the associated training programmes.

These recommendations address India's long-term agenda for AI systems that are locally trained, locally validated, and governed under Indian accountability standards—the point at which data-set geography becomes a solved problem rather than a disclosed limitation.
Responsible Actors: IndiaAI Mission, MeitY, sector ministries, and the scientific and academic establishment.

AI systems deployed within India's sovereign digital public infrastructure—Aadhaar-linked services, Ayushman Bharat, PM-KISAN, welfare delivery platforms, and national security systems should, over a defined transition period, be required to demonstrate training data adequacy for the Indian population and context. The National Data Governance Framework should be explicitly linked to AI training data-set standards, with MeitY and the IndiaAI Mission jointly defining the adequacy criteria for each domain.[11][12][13]

The IndiaAI Mission should prioritise the development of foundational AI models trained on Indian languages, clinical data, legal corpora, agricultural data sets, and Indian governance frameworks. These models are not substitutes for general-purpose AI—they are the contextually validated layer that makes general-purpose AI deployable with confidence in Indian institutional environments. Funding should be commensurate with the strategic importance of this agenda, drawing on the IndiaAI Mission's compute infrastructure and research network.[14]
• Develop Indigenous Knowledge Integration Frameworks

India's traditional knowledge systems—Ayurveda and traditional medicine, ecological and agricultural knowledge, indigenous governance frameworks, regional legal traditions—represent a validated body of contextual understanding that neither foreign AI systems nor early-stage sovereign models currently incorporate. The Ministry of Culture, in coordination with the Ministry of Science and Technology and the IndiaAI Mission, should establish a structured programme for digitising, validating, and integrating indigenous knowledge into India's AI training data sets, with appropriate attribution and intellectual property protections.[15]

India should use its G20 presidency legacy, its leadership of the Global South coalition, and its engagement in the UN AI governance process to actively advocate for the principles in this framework (mandatory platform disclosure, contextual sovereignty, attribution integrity, and operational accountability) as the governance standard for AI deployment in complex, plural, developing societies. The Ministry of External Affairs, in coordination with MeitY, should develop India's international AI governance position as a coherent strategic doctrine, not a reactive response to EU or US regulatory developments.[16][17]

The history of consequential technologies offers a consistent lesson that capability without accountability does not self-correct. Aviation did not become safe because aircraft became more sophisticated; it was because societies built layered accountability structures consisting of certification, black boxes, incident reporting, and independent investigation, all of which made failures visible, attributable, and correctable. The finance sector did not become stable through better mathematics; this happened through supervisory frameworks and architectures that imposed accountability at the point of consequential actions. AI is not exempt from this logic; instead, the technology is subject to it more urgently than most, because the speed, scale, and opacity of AI-mediated decisions compress the window in which human correction is possible.

The AI Handler Doctrine does not propose to slow AI down. It proposes to make the technology accountable in the way that every other high-consequence institutional actor already is, be it a surgeon, an auditor, a commanding officer, or a judge. Each is subject to a designated responsibility, supervisory review, and a structured redressal when things go wrong.

For India, the stakes are specific and immediate. As AI integrates with Aadhaar, UPI, and the large Indian DPI, their outputs will increasingly shape access to credit, welfare entitlements, health diagnoses, and civic rights for hundreds of millions of people. A contextual failure at that scale is not a technology incident. It is a governance failure.

The age of AI will define the institutional character of this century. Whether that century is one of accountable governance or of diffused, unattributable algorithmic authority is a choice that is still available to sovereign nations, but not indefinitely.

India has the institutional depth, the democratic mandate, and the information infrastructure to lead on this question. The AI Handler Doctrine is one framework for doing so. However, the question can no longer be deferred.

While the common man and commercial enterprises may initially perceive AI as a frictionless and near-ultimate solution to systemic challenges, this enthusiasm must be grounded in operational safety. The introduction of the AI Handler framework will ensure that when the citizen relies on an AI output for their health, livelihood, or rights, they are protected by an institutional guarantee of reliability and recourse.
